doing it.
And then several years later this friend that I went with had a bead store in the town
where I live in Idaho in the U.S.
And she asked me to teach classes and I said, you know, I really don't want to.
It was not fun at all.
I didn't enjoy it.
But she kept talking and talking to me about it and I finally agreed and we had a class
and it was difficult for the students to do it the old way.
So I sat down with my husband and we thought about the different ways that we could improve
the experience, one being that if we could just start weaving immediately and we came
up with a lazy, lazy tool.
Because it gives you an immediate satisfaction, I think doing the weave itself is very
restful and it's something that's very portable, something you can take with you easily.
Stick in your pocket, you can go on the train with it or if you're sitting waiting for
someone and it's an ancient technique and a quick technique and it just lends itself
to doing a lot of different types of design with wire.
So it's kind of an uncharted territory now that we have the tool everyone's able to
make it faster.
So we're seeing some really great designs coming up.
The different types of materials I like to use are the wires.
I haven't found anything else that really works well with this particular tool other
than wire so it's really geared towards that.
And I like to stay in the range, the US range would be like a 24 to 26 gauge wire.
However my husband likes to work with the heavier gauges of wire in the 20 gauge and
it can look more like a chain mail project.
So anything, any kind of wire that will hold its shape can be used on the lazy daisy on
either of the tools.
I have been jewelry making for probably 50 years a long time.
